# Can LLM Agents Be Forward-Deployed Engineers? Requirement Discovery and Delivery for Enterprise Text-to-SQL

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#fde-requirement-discovery)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03551v1) · arXiv v1, 2 November 2026

**Reading coverage:** All 27 public PDF pages: main sections 1–5; limitations; Appendices A–L including discovery protocol, published fact-sheet description, scoring audit, open-decision case study, delivery setup, repeat-run failures, resource reconciliation and complete displayed prompts. No private engagement records or linked code were accessed.

## Research question

An enterprise SQL system must satisfy requirements that customers initially leave vague, and benchmark accuracy alone may miss deployment constraints.

## Method

A fact-sheet-grounded customer simulator supports discovery of 17 known requirements while preserving six explicitly unknown decisions. Agents submit requirements and then use autonomous or separated planning/execution workflows to post-train and profile an Oracle-dialect SQL model under stated resource limits.

## Evaluation

Discovery covers 15 models, three disclosure levels and ten runs per condition. Delivery compares eight model/workflow configurations, with a separate harness comparison and repeated GPT-6.1 runs. Acceptance combines Spider-dev accuracy, compilation failures on 100 production questions and CPU p90 latency; BIRD is report-only.

## What the results support

Automatic judgments report roughly 60% pooled recovery and over 80% for leading discovery models. Two of eight selected delivery results pass all three gates. Repeated GPT-6.1 trials complete training in three of six runs and pass once, illustrating that completion and acceptance differ.

## Limits and qualifications

This is one enterprise engagement with simulated customers and a historical human reference. Discovery label agreement is 70.6% for recovery on only 51 audited fact instances. Production questions lack reference SQL, so compilation does not measure their semantic accuracy. The 25% figure describes selected configuration results, not a broad success-rate estimate; open measurement choices, differing reasoning budgets and reported resource-allocation deviations constrain causal comparison.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Extends clarification research from individual SQL requests to deployment requirements and their handoff, highlighting unresolved decisions, fact loss and the gap between benchmark quality and operational acceptance.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

| Claim or inference examined | Original evidence | Location | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 25% is a general autonomous-deployment success rate. | Table 2 reports eight selected model/workflow results; Appendix F separately reports six repeated GPT-6.1 runs with only one pass, and the study covers one engagement. | §4.3/Table 2; Appendix F/Table 11; Limitations | Restrict to the reported case-study configuration results. |
| Production acceptance proves production SQL correctness. | The production workload has no reference SQL, and the production metric is cursor-parse/compilation under an explicitly provisional protocol. | Appendix B, pp. 11–12; Appendix D, pp. 13–14 | Distinguish compilation validity and latency from semantic execution accuracy. |
| Discovery scores are thoroughly human-validated. | Human validation of source requirements differs from the scoring audit: the latter covers one trajectory for each of three models, with 36/51 recovery-label agreements. | Appendix C, Table 8 | State the narrow audit and residual judge uncertainty; do not generalize its bias direction to the full cohort. |
